name: Money maxxing / career maxxing

lead: Money maxxing and career maxxing mean pursuing income and professional success as a route to status and attractiveness, especially for men who see their looks as fixed.

The chain: higher income and career standing give status and resources, which raise perceived desirability and also pay for grooming, clothes, skincare and procedures. Evolutionary-psychology research reports that mate preferences track status and resources, and one cited study found higher-salaried men rated more attractive. Research also links perceived attractiveness to employment outcomes.

paras: People pursue promotions, higher-paying skills, businesses or investing, then spend part of the gains on appearance. It runs alongside or instead of looks work and plays out over years.
No direct health risks. Outcomes vary by person and culture, and the research findings are correlational.

chain: Offset or outweigh looks in dating
angle.text: Looksmaxxing and manosphere communities present income and career success as a route to attractiveness: status and resources raise desirability and also pay for appearance upgrades. Mate-preference research partly supports a link between status and desirability.

lead: Money maxxing and career maxxing describe the idea in looksmaxxing and manosphere communities that income, wealth and professional success can compensate for, or substitute for, physical attractiveness. It is often presented as an alternative route to status for men who consider their looks fixed.

Research in evolutionary psychology reports that women's mate preferences track indicators of status and resources, and one cited study found that higher-salaried men were rated more attractive.[1] Wikipedia also notes research linking perceived attractiveness to employment outcomes.[1] Whether deliberate career or money strategies change dating outcomes has not been tested as a looksmaxxing practice.

paras: Status is the relative social value attributed to a person, and socioeconomic status is typically indexed by income, education and occupational prestige.[2] Reference works report that women's preferences for male partners track status cues such as resources and dominance, and that attractiveness affects hiring and social opportunities.[1] Evolutionary psychologists describe prestige as more important to male attractiveness than dominance.[3]

Forum members describe "money maxxing" as a way to afford grooming, procedures and clothing, and as an independent source of attractiveness; others dispute how much money can offset looks. These are community positions, not research findings.
No studies found. Related economics and psychology literature on the attractiveness-income link exists but does not evaluate this practice.
